title: 7. Why the Price Is What It Is: Valuation, Reverse DCF & Peer Comps

epigraph.quote: A low headline multiple is not a margin of safety when earnings are flattered by one-time tax benefits and the market is debating what replaces a departing flagship customer.
epigraph.author: Valuation Discipline

web_blocks.html: At the November 13, 2026 close of $172.47, Qualcomm carries a $184.54 billion market cap and $192.85 billion Enterprise Value [23]. On surface multiples, shares look cheap: 13.58x trailing GAAP P/E, 14.24x forward P/E, 0.92x PEG, and 4.47x EV/Sales [23]. Yet two quirks distort those ratios. First, trailing GAAP Net Income of $13.63 billion benefited from a $4.21 billion one-time tax gain [3]. Underlying FY26 operating earnings were roughly 30% lower [3]. Second, Wall Street models a near-term profit trough in FY2027. Consensus sees FY27 revenue near $45.42B ($44.31B–$47.75B) and non-GAAP EPS of $9.59–$9.71 as Apple ramps its C2 modem and wafer costs rise [26]. In FY2028, consensus rebounds to ~$52.45B in sales and ~$12.11–$12.21 in EPS as Data Center, Auto, and IoT scale [26].

web_blocks.caption: Table 7.1: Semiconductor & Custom-Silicon Peer Valuation Matrix (As of November 13, 2026)
web_blocks.takeaway: Qualcomm trades at 14.24x forward P/E and 4.47x EV/Sales despite posting the peer group's top ROIC (31.13%). That is a steep discount to AI leaders Broadcom (17.96x Fwd P/E, 18.99x EV/Sales) and Marvell (21.53x Fwd P/E, 14.71x EV/Sales).

web_blocks.html: Why does a 31.13%-ROIC chipmaker trade at one-quarter of Broadcom's EV/Sales (18.99x) and under a third of Marvell's (14.71x)? Meanwhile, Qualcomm sits right next to NXP Semiconductors (14.44x forward P/E, 5.38x EV/Sales, 14.63% ROIC) and above Skyworks Solutions (11.87x forward P/E, 5.35x EV/Sales, 2.07% ROIC) [23, 25]. The market is pricing in a handset-erosion discount. Broadcom and Marvell already earn huge revenue from cloud AI ASICs and optical networking (+85.5% and +36.55% quarterly sales growth) [25]. By contrast, Qualcomm's Q4 FY26 sales fell 8.41% YoY [25]. Its $5.0 billion FY2027 Data Center goal (>$650M in Q1 FY27) and AWS custom-silicon/1.6T optical deal are still in early ramp [5, 6, 16].

web_blocks.takeaway: Qualcomm's 14.24x forward P/E actually prices FY2028 recovery EPS (~$12.15). On FY2027 trough estimates (~$9.65), shares trade at a fuller 17.87x.

web_blocks.takeaway: At $172.47, Qualcomm prices in ~6.5%–7.3% annual headline FCF growth. Deducting $3.45B in Stock-Based Compensation lifts that implied economic FCF hurdle to ~12.5% per year.

web_blocks.caption: Table 7.4: Intrinsic Value Sensitivity Matrix (10-Year DCF on $9.25B Normalized Core FCF, 3.0% Terminal g)
web_blocks.takeaway: Every 100 bps of WACC or 250 bps of FCF growth shifts fair value by ~$20–$35 per share. Buying near $152–$157 builds in a 10.5% discount-rate margin of safety.

web_blocks.the_number: $195.00 Base Intrinsic Value (~16.0x FY28E Non-GAAP EPS of $12.15, or ~21x Normalized FCF)
web_blocks.how_calculated: We anchor on FY2028 consensus Non-GAAP EPS (~$12.11–$12.21) rather than depressed FY2027 trough EPS (~$9.65) or tax-distorted FY2026 GAAP EPS ($12.70), applying a 16.0x multiple—a modest premium to NXP (14.44x) for Qualcomm's superior 31.1% ROIC and QTL cash vault, yet still a 10%–25% discount to Broadcom (17.96x) and Marvell (21.53x).
web_blocks.the_inputs: FY28E Revenue $52.45B; QCT EBT margin recovering toward 28%–29% on Data Center scale and memory-cost pass-through; QTL steady at ~$5.2B–$5.5B revenue (~72% EBT margin); diluted shares ~1,030M–1,045M after net buybacks.
web_blocks.the_range: Bear $130.00 (13.5x stalled ~$9.50 EPS if Data Center slips and handset erosion deepens) to Bull $245.00 (19.5x ~$12.55 EPS if Data Center beats $5B and Arm royalty suspension adds ~$300M/yr).
web_blocks.if_off: If FY27 Data Center revenue misses the $5B trajectory or gross margins compress further under memory/warrant pressure, the multiple will remain pinned at 13x–14x on ~$9.50–$10.00 EPS ($125–$140).

web_blocks.mechanism: Pivoted away from mature, customer-concentrated mobile and consumer storage controllers into hyperscale cloud, 5G carrier, and custom data-center optical/ASIC silicon through organic R&D and targeted IP acquisitions.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: Expanded data-center/cloud mix from under 25% to >50% of revenue as sales grew from ~$2.4B to ~$5.9B, triggering a valuation re-rating from ~14x forward P/E to >25x forward P/E.
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: A legacy connectivity chipmaker only earns an infrastructure multiple after non-handset revenue proves durable >50% mix and gross-margin accretion—not on management's initial slide-deck guidance.

web_blocks.html: Sum-of-the-Parts (SOTP) Valuation Cross-Check: We also test our $195.00 Base Case by valuing both segments separately on FY2028E earnings. QTL (Licensing) earns ~$5.2B–$5.5B in sales at a ~72% EBT margin (~$3.8B–$4.0B EBT). At a 14%–15% tax rate, that yields ~$3.3B in after-tax profit. A conservative 14x–15x royalty multiple values QTL alone at $46B–$50B (~$44–$47/share). QCT (Chips) is modeled at ~$47.0B in FY28E sales and a 28% EBT margin (~$13.1B EBT, ~$11.2B after-tax). Applying 14x–15x—below Broadcom (17.96x) and Marvell (21.53x)—values QCT at $157B–$168B (~$150–$160/share). Subtracting ~$7.4B in net debt (~$7/share) yields an SOTP range of $187–$200/share, backing our $195.00 Base Case.

web_blocks.title: Why Dividend Yield & Buybacks Cushion Downside Without Creating Near-Term Upside
paragraphs: Qualcomm's $3.62 TTM dividend ($3.77 forward, 2.19% yield) and $6.81B buyback program support shares near 13x–14x forward earnings [3, 23].

Still, $3.45B in Stock-Based Compensation eats ~51% of gross buybacks, leaving ~2.5%–3.0% net share shrinkage per year [3]. That helps 5-year EPS compounding, but cannot lift the multiple while Q4 Handsets fall 26% YoY [7].

web_blocks.html: What the Market Needs to Re-Rate QCOM From 14x to 18x+: Qualcomm traded at 12x–15x forward earnings during phone-only cycles (2015–2019). It reached 18x–22x only during the 2020–2022 5G super-cycle [17]. To earn an infrastructure multiple near Broadcom (17.96x) or Marvell (21.53x), Qualcomm must clear three FY2027 hurdles. First, Q1 FY27 Data Center sales (>$650M) must scale toward $5.0B without pulling QCT gross margin under 50%. Second, 2H FY27 price hikes must offset memory and wafer inflation [8]. Third, inventory days must drop from 156 DIO back toward 115–125 DIO, releasing $1.5B–$2.0B of trapped cash.

Why the 0.92 PEG Ratio Requires Context: QCOM's 0.92 PEG ratio (14.24x forward P/E over 15.53% 5-year EPS growth) looks cheap against peers [23]. However, that growth is back-loaded into FY2028–FY2029 ($52.45B FY28 sales, $12.15 EPS), not FY2027 (-8.05% EPS dip) [23, 26]. Paying $172.47 today (17.87x FY27 trough EPS) leaves thin room for error. Buying near $152.37–$157.01 (15.8x–16.3x FY27 EPS, ~12.7x FY28E EPS) builds a real margin of safety.

Bottom Line on Valuation: At $172.47, QCOM is fairly priced for a transitional FY2027 bridge year. It offers ~13% upside to our $195.00 Base Case, but demands ~12.5% SBC-adjusted FCF growth over ten years. Waiting for $152.37–$157.01 turns a fair-value debate into a 5.47:1 asymmetric bet.

Our $152.37–$157.01 support zone also aligns with FY2027 trough valuation math [24, 25]. That range values QCOM at 15.8x–16.3x FY2027 consensus EPS of $9.65, while our $195.00 base target prices 16.0x FY2028E EPS of $12.15 [25].

book_paragraphs: Now you and I leave the price-blind room and open the quote screen. As of the November 13, 2026 session close, Qualcomm trades at $172.47 per share, giving the company a market capitalization of $184.54 billion and an Enterprise Value of $192.85 billion after accounting for roughly $7.4 billion to $8.3 billion in net debt. At first glance, the valuation screen flashes what looks like a classic value-investor gift: 13.58 times trailing GAAP earnings, 14.24 times forward earnings, a 0.92 PEG ratio, and 4.47 times EV-to-Sales, all for a business generating a 31.1 percent Return on Invested Capital and paying a 2.1 percent dividend yield.

Before you reach for your wallet, let us dissect why the market has parked Qualcomm at $172.47—more than 33 percent below its 52-week high of $259.92—while Wall Street's average price target sits modestly higher around $188.01. Notice the extraordinary dispersion beneath that $188 average: bearish analysts sit between $100 and $150, while bullish analysts reach $280 to $320. When a high-ROIC technology leader trades at 14 times forward earnings with a $220 target spread in the middle of an AI infrastructure boom, the market is rarely asleep. It is pricing in a genuine structural debate.

The first piece of that debate is earnings quality. That 13.58 times trailing P/E sits on $13.63 billion of FY2026 GAAP Net Income, which was artificially lifted by a $4.21 billion one-time income-tax windfall even as GAAP operating income fell 30 percent to $8.66 billion. If you strip out that tax benefit, trailing operating earnings tell a much more sober story. Second, Wall Street consensus expects FY2027 to be a bridge year rather than an immediate breakout: analysts model FY2027 revenue of roughly $45.42 billion and non-GAAP EPS of $9.59 to $9.71, because Apple's internal C2 modem is taking share inside the iPhone 18 lineup while rising memory and wafer costs squeeze near-term QCT margins. Notice what that means for the multiple: at $172.47, Qualcomm is actually trading at nearly 17.9 times FY2027 trough consensus earnings, and 14.2 times FY2028 recovery consensus of $12.15 per share.

Third, let us walk through our peer comparison table so you can see exactly how institutional capital is pricing each semiconductor business model. At the top of the table sits Broadcom at $347.01, commanding 17.96 times forward earnings and 18.99 times EV-to-Sales on 24.4 percent ROIC and 66.5 percent gross margins—because Broadcom's quarterly sales are surging 85.5 percent on proven hyperscale AI accelerators. Next sits Marvell Technology at $156.76, trading at 21.53 times forward earnings and 14.71 times EV-to-Sales on 36.6 percent quarterly sales growth. Then look at the other end of the table: NXP Semiconductors trades at 14.44 times forward earnings and 5.38 times EV-to-Sales with 14.6 percent ROIC, and RF supplier Skyworks Solutions trades at 11.87 times forward earnings with just 2.1 percent ROIC.

Where has the market placed Qualcomm? Right next to NXP—at 14.24 times forward earnings and 4.47 times EV-to-Sales—despite Qualcomm's superior 31.1 percent ROIC and 72-percent-margin patent vault. The message from the market is unmistakable: until Qualcomm proves that its $5 billion FY2027 Data Center target and AWS custom-silicon partnership can scale at healthy margins, investors will value QCOM as a cyclical handset-and-auto supplier rather than an AI infrastructure compounder.

To test what is actually baked into $172.47 without relying on relative multiples, let us run a Reverse Discounted Cash Flow model. Using a 9.5 percent weighted average cost of capital and a 3.0 percent terminal growth rate, an Enterprise Value of $192.85 billion implies that Qualcomm must grow its FY2026 reported Free Cash Flow of $8.65 billion at roughly 7.3 percent per year for the next decade, reaching about $17.5 billion by FY2036. If we strip out FY2026's $2.11 billion inventory build to use a normalized core FCF baseline of $9.25 billion, the implied 10-year FCF growth rate drops to 6.5 percent per year. On reported cash flow, that is a very reasonable hurdle—if Automotive marches toward its $8 billion FY2029 target and Data Center delivers.

However, remember our forensic lesson from Chapter 6 about Stock-Based Compensation. Qualcomm paid out $3.45 billion in SBC in FY2026—8 percent of revenue—absorbing half of its $6.81 billion in share repurchases. If you deduct SBC from Free Cash Flow to measure true economic cash flow available to outside owners ($5.20 billion), the Reverse DCF math changes dramatically: at $172.47, you are demanding roughly 12.5 percent annual economic FCF growth for ten years. Furthermore, look at our DCF sensitivity table: if the market's required return rises by just one percentage point to 10.5 percent while FCF compounds at 6.5 percent, intrinsic value drops to $151.90. That is why buying at $172.47 leaves very little margin of safety, whereas buying near $152 to $157 builds in a genuine 10.5 percent discount-rate cushion.

Our base intrinsic value estimate lands at $195.00 per share, built on 16.0 times FY2028 consensus non-GAAP EPS of $12.15—a modest premium to NXP for Qualcomm's elite ROIC, yet still a meaningful discount to Broadcom and Marvell. Consider the historical parallel of Marvell Technology between 2016 and 2022. Marvell was once priced at 14 times forward earnings as a mature storage and mobile connectivity supplier. It only earned a sustained re-rating above 25 times forward earnings after cloud and data-center silicon crossed 50 percent of revenue and proved accretive to gross margins. Qualcomm is standing at that exact same threshold in late 2026: its fundamentals are transitioning in the right direction, yet the market will not pay an AI multiple until the December-quarter $650 million Data Center print and 2H FY27 margin recovery show up in audited numbers.

Let us cross-check that $195.00 Base Case using a Sum-of-the-Parts lens, because Qualcomm is really two very different businesses bolted together. First, look at QTL, the patent licensing vault. With multi-year renewals locked in across Apple, Huawei, and Transsion, QTL generates roughly $5.2 billion to $5.5 billion in annual revenue at a 72 percent pre-tax margin—nearly $4 billion in pre-tax profit, or about $3.3 billion after tax. Even if you value that annuity-like royalty stream at a conservative 14 to 15 times earnings, QTL alone is worth $46 billion to $50 billion, or roughly $45 per share. Now turn to QCT, the semiconductor arm. On fiscal 2028 consensus revenue near $47 billion and a recovering 28 percent pre-tax margin, QCT produces around $11.2 billion in after-tax profit. Value QCT at 14 to 15 times earnings—still a clear discount to Broadcom and Marvell—and you get $157 billion to $168 billion, or $150 to $160 per share. Subtract $7.4 billion in net debt, and your Sum-of-the-Parts value lands squarely between $187 and $200 per share.

Why, then, does the stock sit at $172.47 instead of $195.00 today? Because Wall Street refuses to pay for fiscal 2028 earnings two years early while fiscal 2027 carries genuine execution friction. Specifically, investors want to see three things before awarding that 16-times-plus multiple: first, that Q1 fiscal 2027 Data Center revenue clears the $650 million bar without cratering QCT gross margins; second, that Qualcomm's price increases in the second half of fiscal 2027 successfully offset rising memory and wafer costs; and third, that the $8.64 billion inventory pile begins converting back into cash. Until those milestones hit the tape, the dividend yield of 2.1 percent and net buybacks of roughly 2.5 to 3 percent per year act as a valuation floor rather than a catalyst for immediate upside.

That brings us to the practical takeaway of Chapter 7. Valuation at $172.47 is neither egregiously expensive nor a screaming steal. It is fairly priced for a transitional bridge year, with real medium-term upside to $195 or $245 if Data Center and Automotive execute—but with a much wider margin of safety if we can acquire shares closer to $152 to $157, where the market is effectively pricing Qualcomm at an implied 10.5 percent discount rate and giving us the AI Data Center ramp nearly for free.

book_callouts.title: THE REVERSE DCF VERDICT
book_callouts.text: At $172.47, QCOM prices in ~6.5%–7.3% annual headline FCF growth, which is reasonable—but on SBC-adjusted economic FCF (~$5.20B), the market still demands ~12.5% annual compounding.

book_subsections.title: Deep Dive: Historical Valuation Bands & The Three Re-Rating Hurdles
paragraphs: Let us zoom out for a moment and examine Qualcomm's valuation history over the last decade, because multiples rarely expand in a vacuum. Between fiscal 2015 and fiscal 2019, when investors viewed Qualcomm strictly as a mature smartphone modem vendor embroiled in licensing disputes, the stock spent most of its time oscillating between 12 and 15 times forward earnings. Every rally above 16 times was sold until the 5G super-cycle arrived in 2020 and 2021, pushing operating income from $6.26 billion to $15.86 billion and lifting the forward multiple toward 18 to 22 times. When smartphone demand cooled in 2023 and Apple's internal modem timeline became unmistakable, the multiple compressed right back into the 13 to 15 times band.

That history explains why $172.47—at 14.24 times FY2028 consensus earnings and nearly 18 times FY2027 trough earnings—is a classic show-me price. Wall Street has seen Qualcomm execute brilliantly in Automotive, growing that segment to $6 billion in fiscal 2026, and in IoT at $7.13 billion. Yet Automotive and IoT together still represent roughly $13.1 billion of a $43.1 billion revenue base, while Handsets remain over $24 billion. To break out of its historical 13-to-15-times handset valuation box and earn a multiple closer to Broadcom's 18 times or Marvell's 21.5 times, Qualcomm must clear three concrete hurdles during fiscal 2027.

First, December-quarter Data Center revenue must beat the $650 million bar and show a clear quarterly cadence toward $5 billion for the full fiscal year, without dragging QCT's blended gross margin below 50 percent. Second, management's planned price increases in the second half of fiscal 2027 must visibly offset higher DRAM, HBM, and leading-edge foundry wafer costs so QCT pre-tax margins recover back toward 28 to 30 percent. Third, Qualcomm must work down its $8.64 billion inventory pile—currently sitting at 156 days—back toward 120 days, which alone would release roughly $1.5 billion to $2 billion of trapped cash back onto the balance sheet. If all three happen, $195 to $245 is well within reach; if they stall, 13 to 14 times earnings keeps the stock anchored.

Let us also address a subtle point that trips up many semiconductor investors: why a 0.92 PEG ratio can still be misleading during a customer transition. Standard PEG ratios divide forward P/E by a five-year consensus EPS growth estimate—here, roughly 15.5 percent—which makes Qualcomm look cheaper than 1.0x growth. That five-year growth rate, however, is heavily back-end loaded into fiscal 2028 and fiscal 2029, assuming Automotive reaches $8 billion, IoT reaches $14 billion, and Data Center scales past $5 billion toward $15 billion. In the near term, fiscal 2027 EPS is actually contracting roughly 8 percent before rebounding 25 percent in fiscal 2028. That is why paying 17.9 times fiscal 2027 trough earnings at $172.47 requires patience, whereas stepping in near $152 to $157 drops the trough multiple to 15.8 times and gives you genuine asymmetric protection while the transition plays out.

To make that valuation gap tangible, compare two entry points side by side. If you buy Qualcomm today at $172.47 and fiscal 2028 earnings hit our $12.15 Base Case at a 16-times multiple ($195.00), your cumulative upside over eighteen months is 13.1 percent—barely compensating you for the risk that Data Center slips or memory costs stay elevated. By contrast, if you wait for the $152.37 to $157.01 support shelf, your Base Case return jumps to 24.2 percent against just $6.94 of downside to the $150.07 stop. Same business, same management team, same $5 billion Data Center target—yet patience transforms a mediocre 1-to-1 bet into a 5.47-to-1 institutional pitch.

Keep that contrast in mind as we move into Chapter 8's technical chart analysis. Valuation tells us what Qualcomm is worth over the next eighteen months—around $195 in our Base Case, with $130 Bear and $245 Bull bookends—but it never tells us when institutional buyers are ready to step in and defend the stock. For timing, we need the tape.
